slides.say: Of a hospital's nurses, one third work night shifts, three quarters drive to work, one quarter are new, and one half work part time. Which statement is not necessarily true?

Every choice says that at least one nurse is in two groups at once. So every choice claims that an overlap must exist. We need the one claim that is not forced. We'll solve it in two different ways, by adding fractions, and then in percent.

Let's start with the math way. When must an overlap exist? Remember the smallest overlap. Only when the two groups add up to more than the total. Here the givens are fractions, so like in the lesson, the total is one.
at: Only when the two groups add up

slides.say: Choice number one says, at least one nurse who is not new does not work night shifts. Not new is one minus a quarter, three quarters. Not nights is one minus a third, two thirds.
at: Not new is one minus a quarter
Not nights is one minus a third

slides.say: Three quarters is nine twelfths, and two thirds is eight twelfths. Together, that's seventeen twelfths. That's more than one, so an overlap must exist.
So the statement is true. They ask for the one that's not necessarily true, so choice number one is out.
at: so choice number one is out

slides.say: Choice number two says, at least one night-shift nurse drives to work. A third plus three quarters. Four twelfths plus nine twelfths is thirteen twelfths. More than one, so it's true, and choice number two is out.
at: so it's true, and choice number two

slides.say: Choice number three says, at least one new nurse drives to work. A quarter plus three quarters is exactly one. It's not more than one.

Exactly one doesn't force an overlap. The two groups can sit side by side. Let's see it in numbers. Say there are twelve nurses, because twelve splits into thirds and quarters. A quarter, three, are new. Three quarters, nine, drive.
The three new nurses come by bus, and the other nine drive. Every fraction still works, and no new nurse drives. So choice number three is not necessarily true.

In the exam you'd circle it and move on. Here, let's check the last one too. Choice number four says, at least one part-time nurse does not work night shifts. A half plus two thirds is three sixths plus four sixths, seven sixths. More than one, so it's true.
at: More than one, so it's true

slides.say: Choice number three is our answer. And if two groups add up to less than one, then no overlap is forced either. The smallest overlap is zero, never negative.
at: Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now an insight, the one from the lesson. We can compare with a hundred percent instead of one. We start again from the givens, and turn every fraction into percent. Again, we need the claim that isn't forced.

A third is thirty-three and a third percent. Let's write just thirty-three, and in a moment we'll see why that's fine. Three quarters is seventy-five percent. A quarter is twenty-five percent, and a half is fifty percent.
Not new is a hundred minus twenty-five, seventy-five. Not nights is a hundred minus thirty-three, sixty-seven.
at: Not new is a hundred minus twenty-five
Not nights is a hundred minus thirty-three

slides.say: Choice number one says at least one nurse who is not new does not work night shifts. Seventy-five plus sixty-seven is a hundred forty-two. That's more than a hundred, so the overlap is forced. Choice number two says at least one night-shift nurse drives to work. Thirty-three plus seventy-five is a hundred eight. Again, the overlap is forced.

Now, why could we drop the third of a percent? With it, choice number two would be a hundred eight and a third. Dropping the third changes a sum by less than one. So it matters only when the sum lands right next to a hundred, like ninety-nine and a bit. A hundred eight is far above a hundred, so the overlap is forced with or without the third.
at: With it, choice number two would be

slides.say: Choice number three says at least one new nurse drives to work. Twenty-five plus seventy-five is exactly a hundred, so the overlap isn't forced. Choice number four says at least one part-time nurse does not work night shifts. Fifty plus sixty-seven is a hundred seventeen, more than a hundred. That overlap is forced.
Here fractions or percents show which overlap is forced. Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number three is our answer
